questions.stem: Which plant tissue carries water and dissolved minerals up from the roots to the leaves?
options: Palisade mesophyll
Epidermis
Xylem
Phloem
questions.explanation: Xylem vessels are hollow tubes of dead, lignified cells that carry water and minerals upward. Phloem carries sugars made in photosynthesis, in either direction, through living sieve tube cells.

questions.stem: What is the main function of phloem in a vascular plant?
options: Transporting sugars from where they are made or stored to where they are used
Transporting water and minerals from the roots up to the leaves
Supporting the stem with thick walls of dead cells strengthened by lignin
Exchanging carbon dioxide and oxygen with the air through pores in the leaf surface
questions.explanation: Phloem moves sugars such as sucrose from sources, like leaves, to sinks, like roots, fruits and growing tips. Moving water up from the roots, and support from lignified walls, are roles of xylem. Gas exchange happens through stomata.

questions.stem: How is a root hair cell specialised for absorbing water?
options: A long, thin extension gives it a large surface area in contact with soil water
Its many chloroplasts make sugar to draw water in by photosynthesis
Its thick, waxy cuticle stops the water it has absorbed from leaking back out into the soil
Its lignified walls form a hollow tube that carries water upward
questions.explanation: The hair-like extension greatly increases surface area for water to enter by osmosis. Root hair cells are underground and have no chloroplasts. A waxy cuticle would block water uptake, and hollow lignified tubes describe xylem vessels.

questions.stem: Xylem vessels are made of dead cells with no end walls, whereas phloem sieve tubes are living cells supported by companion cells. Why does this difference suit their functions?
options: Xylem flow is driven by transpiration, while phloem transport needs energy from living cells
Xylem flow needs ATP from living cells, while phloem moves sugars passively by evaporation
Xylem must make sugars as it carries water, while phloem only carries water and minerals
Xylem cells divide to push water upward, while phloem cells die to form an open tube
questions.explanation: Water moves through xylem passively, pulled up by transpiration, so open dead tubes give the least resistance. Loading sugars into phloem requires energy, which living companion cells supply. Neither tissue makes sugar.

questions.stem: What is transpiration?
options: The uptake of water by root hair cells through osmosis
The release of oxygen gas from the leaves as a by-product of photosynthesis
The loss of water vapour from a plant, mostly through its stomata
The transport of sugars through the phloem to the roots
questions.explanation: Transpiration is evaporation of water from the leaves, mainly through open stomata. This loss creates the pull that draws water up the xylem. Water uptake by roots is the start of the pathway, not transpiration itself.

questions.stem: Which model best explains how water moves from the roots to the top of a tall tree?
options: Water is drawn up the phloem by the sugars it carries down from the leaves
Transpiration creates tension, pulling a cohesive column of water up the xylem
Root pressure alone pushes water to the top of the tree through the phloem
Active transport pumps water from xylem cell to xylem cell up the stem
questions.explanation: As water evaporates from leaves, it pulls on the water column in the xylem; cohesion between water molecules and adhesion to vessel walls keep the column unbroken. Root pressure is far too weak to lift water up a tall tree, and xylem cells are dead, so they cannot pump.

questions.stem: A leafy shoot is set up in a potometer, which measures water uptake. Which change would most increase the rate of uptake?
options: Coating the underside of every leaf with petroleum jelly
Moving the shoot from warm, dry, moving air into cool, still, humid air
Moving the shoot from still, humid air to warm, dry, moving air
Moving the shoot from bright light into complete darkness
questions.explanation: Warm, dry, moving air increases evaporation from the leaves, so transpiration and water uptake rise. Darkness closes stomata, petroleum jelly blocks the stomata on the underside where most are found, and humid air reduces the gradient for evaporation, so each lowers uptake.

questions.stem: What is the correct order of levels of organisation in an animal, from smallest to largest?
options: Tissue, cell, organ, system
Cell, organ, tissue, system
Organ, tissue, cell, system
Cell, tissue, organ, system
questions.explanation: Similar specialised cells form a tissue, tissues work together in an organ, and organs combine in a system. For example, epithelial and muscle tissues form the stomach, which is part of the digestive system.

questions.stem: Which type of tissue lines the small intestine and the kidney tubules, where its cells are specialised for absorption?
options: Epithelial tissue
Connective tissue
Muscle tissue
Nervous tissue
questions.explanation: Epithelial tissue covers surfaces and lines tubes and cavities; in the intestine and kidney tubules its cells absorb and reabsorb substances, often with microvilli to add surface area. Connective tissue supports and binds other tissues, and muscle tissue contracts.

questions.stem: Where are most of the products of digestion absorbed into the blood?
options: Small intestine
Large intestine
Stomach
Oesophagus
questions.explanation: The small intestine, with its villi and microvilli, absorbs most digested nutrients into the blood and lymph. The large intestine mainly absorbs water and salts, and the oesophagus only moves food to the stomach.

questions.stem: How do villi and microvilli help the small intestine carry out its function?
options: They make hydrochloric acid that kills microorganisms swallowed with the food
They greatly increase the surface area for absorbing nutrients
They secrete bile that breaks fats into smaller droplets
They grind food into smaller pieces by muscular contraction
questions.explanation: Folds, villi and microvilli give the small intestine an enormous surface area, and each villus has a capillary network and thin epithelium, so absorption is fast. Bile is made by the liver, grinding happens in the mouth and stomach, and acid is made in the stomach.

questions.stem: What role does the liver play in digestion?
options: It stores bile made by the pancreas and releases it into the large intestine
It absorbs water from undigested food before it is egested
It produces bile, which emulsifies fats in the small intestine
It produces lipase, which digests fats in the stomach
questions.explanation: The liver makes bile, which the gall bladder stores and releases into the small intestine, where it breaks fat into small droplets for lipase to act on. Bile contains no enzymes. Water is absorbed from undigested material in the large intestine.

questions.stem: The pancreas belongs to both the digestive and endocrine systems. Which statement explains why?
options: It secretes hormones into the small intestine and enzymes into the blood
It secretes enzymes into the small intestine and hormones into the blood
It secretes bile into the small intestine and enzymes into the blood
It absorbs nutrients from food and stores glucose as glycogen
questions.explanation: Pancreatic juice, containing enzymes such as amylase, lipase and proteases, travels by a duct to the small intestine. The islets of Langerhans release insulin and glucagon directly into the blood, which is how endocrine glands deliver hormones. Bile comes from the liver, and glycogen is stored mainly in liver and muscle.

questions.stem: How do endocrine glands deliver their hormones to target cells?
options: They secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream
They release hormones through ducts into body cavities
They pass hormones along nerve axons to target cells
They secrete hormones into the digestive tract
questions.explanation: Endocrine glands are ductless and release hormones into the blood, which carries them throughout the body. Only cells with matching receptors respond. Glands that use ducts, such as salivary glands, are exocrine.

questions.stem: Why do only some cells respond to a hormone that reaches every part of the body in the blood?
options: Hormones are broken down before reaching cells that are not targets
Only target cells take the hormone in by active transport using ATP
Only target cells have receptors that bind that particular hormone
Only target cells are reached by the capillaries that carry the hormone
questions.explanation: A hormone acts only on cells with specific receptors for it, so a target cell is defined by its receptors, not its location. The hormone passes cells without receptors, but they have nothing to bind it, so they do not respond.

questions.stem: Which structure in a nephron filters blood under pressure?
options: Loop of Henle
Collecting duct
Ureter
Glomerulus
questions.explanation: Blood pressure in the glomerulus forces water and small solutes into Bowman's capsule to form filtrate. The loop of Henle and collecting duct reabsorb water and salts from the filtrate, and the ureter carries urine to the bladder.

questions.stem: Glucose is present in the filtrate in Bowman's capsule but is normally absent from urine. What explains this?
options: It is reabsorbed into the blood, mainly in the proximal convoluted tubule
It is too large to pass from the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule
It is broken down by enzymes in the bladder before urine is released
It is secreted back into the filtrate in the collecting duct
questions.explanation: Glucose is small enough to be filtered, but carrier proteins in the proximal convoluted tubule reabsorb all of it into the blood when levels are normal. Proteins and blood cells, not glucose, are too large to be filtered.

questions.stem: Blood plasma, filtrate from Bowman's capsule and urine are tested. Plasma contains protein and glucose; filtrate contains glucose but no protein; urine contains neither but has more urea than filtrate. What does this show?
options: Glucose is filtered and secreted, protein is reabsorbed, and urea is broken down in the bladder
Protein is not filtered, glucose is filtered then reabsorbed, and water is reabsorbed from the filtrate
Protein is reabsorbed in the tubule, glucose is not filtered, and urea is added by the glomerulus
Protein and glucose are both filtered, then both are fully broken down in the loop of Henle
questions.explanation: Protein is too large to pass the glomerulus, so it never reaches the filtrate. Glucose is filtered but reabsorbed. Urea becomes more concentrated because much of the water is reabsorbed along the tubule and collecting duct, leaving the urea in less volume.

questions.stem: What controls the opening and closing of a stoma?
options: The waxy cuticle melting and setting with temperature
Phloem tubes carrying sugar into the cells of the lower epidermis
A pair of guard cells changing shape as they gain or lose water
Xylem vessels pushing water out through the leaf surface
questions.explanation: Each stoma is surrounded by two guard cells. When they take in water and become turgid they curve apart and the pore opens; when they lose water and become flaccid the pore closes.

questions.stem: A plant's roots detect that the soil is drying out. Which response helps the plant conserve water?
options: Xylem vessels close their pores, so water stops reaching the leaves
Abscisic acid is released, causing guard cells to lose water and close the stomata
Abscisic acid is released, causing guard cells to take in water and open the stomata
Guard cells take in potassium ions, so they become turgid and close the stomata
questions.explanation: In water stress the plant produces abscisic acid, which causes potassium ions and then water to leave the guard cells. The guard cells become flaccid and the stomata close, reducing transpiration. Potassium entering guard cells makes them turgid, which opens the stomata.

questions.stem: On a hot, dry afternoon a plant closes its stomata. What is a cost of this response?
options: More sugar leaves the phloem, because transport speeds up
Less carbon dioxide enters the leaf, so photosynthesis slows
More water is lost, because the leaf can no longer cool by transpiration
Less oxygen leaves the leaf, so the plant can no longer respire
questions.explanation: Stomata are the main route for carbon dioxide into the leaf, so closing them to save water also limits photosynthesis. Closing them reduces water loss rather than increasing it. Respiration continues, because the leaf's cells still have oxygen to use.

questions.stem: Most stomata of many plants are on the lower surface of the leaf. How does this help regulate water balance?
options: The lower surface is closer to the xylem, so water reaches it faster
The lower surface has more sunlight, so water evaporates more slowly
The lower surface has a thicker cuticle, so stomata can stay open
The lower surface is shaded and cooler, so less water evaporates through the pores
questions.explanation: The underside of a leaf is out of direct sunlight and usually cooler, so stomata there lose less water by evaporation while still letting carbon dioxide in. The upper surface receives more light, which would increase water loss.

questions.stem: What is homeostasis?
options: Keeping an organism's internal environment within a narrow range
Changing an organism's internal environment to match its surroundings
Keeping body temperature at exactly one value at all times
Responding to an external stimulus by moving away from it
questions.explanation: Homeostasis maintains internal conditions such as temperature, blood glucose and water balance within narrow tolerance limits. The values fluctuate around a set point rather than staying exactly fixed. Matching the surroundings is what homeostasis prevents.

questions.stem: What is the correct order of the parts of a stimulus–response model?
options: Stimulus, receptor, control centre, effector, response
Stimulus, effector, control centre, receptor, response
Receptor, stimulus, effector, control centre, response
Stimulus, control centre, receptor, response, effector
questions.explanation: A change (stimulus) is detected by a receptor, which signals a control centre (also called a modulator) such as the hypothalamus. The control centre signals an effector, a muscle or gland, which carries out the response. Effectors act on information they receive; they do not detect the change.

questions.stem: Why is thermoregulation an example of negative feedback?
options: The response only happens when the body is too cold, never when it is too hot
The response is carried out by receptors rather than effectors
The response reverses the change, returning temperature toward its set point
The response increases the change, moving temperature further from its set point
questions.explanation: In negative feedback the response counteracts the stimulus: a rise in temperature triggers cooling and a fall triggers warming. A response that amplifies the change would be positive feedback, which does not maintain a stable state.

questions.stem: Where are the thermoreceptors that detect a change in core body temperature, and where is the control centre for thermoregulation?
options: Receptors in the hypothalamus; control centre in the hypothalamus
Receptors in the skin; control centre in the thyroid gland
Receptors in the hypothalamus; control centre in the pituitary
Receptors in the skeletal muscles; control centre in the skin
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus contains central thermoreceptors that monitor blood temperature, and it is also the control centre that coordinates responses. Peripheral thermoreceptors in the skin detect skin temperature, but the thyroid and pituitary are not the control centre for temperature.

questions.stem: A person walks into a cold wind. Which set of responses helps keep their core temperature stable?
options: Vasodilation of skin arterioles, sweating and hair erection
Vasoconstriction of skin arterioles, sweating and reduced metabolism
Vasodilation of skin arterioles, shivering and reduced metabolism
Vasoconstriction of skin arterioles, shivering and hair erection
questions.explanation: Narrowing the arterioles to the skin keeps warm blood in the core, shivering generates heat by muscle contraction, and erect hairs trap a layer of air. Vasodilation and sweating are cooling responses that would make heat loss worse.

questions.stem: During a long run on a hot day, a runner's skin becomes flushed and they sweat heavily. How do these two responses each lower body temperature?
options: Vasodilation keeps blood in the core to protect it; sweat absorbs heat as it evaporates
Vasodilation lowers metabolic rate in the skin; sweat removes heat as it drips away
Vasodilation brings blood to the skin to lose heat; sweat absorbs heat as it evaporates
Vasoconstriction brings blood to the skin to lose heat; sweat cools by soaking the skin
questions.explanation: Widened skin arterioles carry more warm blood near the surface, where heat is lost by radiation. Sweat cools only when it evaporates, because evaporation takes heat from the skin; sweat that drips off removes little heat. Vasoconstriction narrows the arterioles and reduces blood flow to the skin.

questions.stem: How does the hypothalamus increase metabolic rate during prolonged cold?
options: It releases insulin, so body cells take up more glucose and release more heat
It releases TRH, so the pituitary releases TSH and the thyroid releases more thyroxine
It releases TSH, so the thyroid releases TRH and the pituitary releases more thyroxine
It releases thyroxine directly, so the liver releases more glucagon into the blood
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus secretes thyrotropin-releasing hormone, which stimulates the anterior pituitary to release thyroid-stimulating hormone. TSH causes the thyroid to secrete thyroxine, which raises the metabolic rate of body cells and so their heat production.

questions.stem: Which cells release insulin when blood glucose rises?
options: Liver cells that store glucose as glycogen
Cells of the adrenal medulla above the kidneys
Beta cells of the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas
Alpha cells of the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas
questions.explanation: Beta cells in the pancreatic islets secrete insulin in response to high blood glucose. Alpha cells in the same islets secrete glucagon when glucose is low. The liver is a target of insulin, not its source.

questions.stem: After a meal high in carbohydrate, what does insulin cause?
options: The kidneys excrete the extra glucose so the blood level returns to normal
Body cells take up more glucose, and the liver converts glucose to glycogen
The liver converts glycogen to glucose and releases it into the blood
Body cells release glucose into the blood, and the liver stores glucagon
questions.explanation: Insulin increases glucose uptake by body cells, especially muscle and fat cells, and stimulates the liver and muscles to store glucose as glycogen, so blood glucose falls. Breaking glycogen down to release glucose is the effect of glucagon. Healthy kidneys reabsorb all filtered glucose.

questions.stem: A student several hours from their last meal plays a long game of football. Which change keeps their blood glucose within its normal range?
options: Alpha cells release glucagon, and muscle cells convert glucose into glycogen
Beta cells release glucagon, and the liver converts glucose into glycogen
Alpha cells release glucagon, and the liver breaks down glycogen into glucose
Beta cells release insulin, and the liver breaks down glycogen into glucose
questions.explanation: Falling blood glucose is detected by the pancreas, and alpha cells release glucagon. Glucagon makes liver cells break down stored glycogen and release glucose into the blood. Insulin would lower blood glucose further, and converting glucose to glycogen removes it from the blood.

questions.stem: Why are insulin and glucagon described as antagonistic hormones?
options: They both act on the kidneys to change how much glucose is excreted
They have opposite effects on the same variable, blood glucose level
They are released by the same cells at the same time after meals
They both raise blood glucose, but in different target organs
questions.explanation: Insulin lowers blood glucose and glucagon raises it, so together they keep it within a narrow range. They come from different cells in the pancreatic islets, beta and alpha cells, and are released under opposite conditions.

questions.stem: Where are the osmoreceptors that detect a rise in blood solute concentration?
options: In the adrenal glands
In the hypothalamus
In the kidney tubules
In the bladder wall
questions.explanation: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus monitor the solute concentration of the blood. When it rises, they trigger thirst and the release of antidiuretic hormone from the posterior pituitary. The kidneys respond to ADH but do not detect the change.

questions.stem: Where is antidiuretic hormone (ADH) made, and where is it released into the blood?
options: Made in the kidney; released from the adrenal glands
Made in the anterior pituitary; released from the thyroid
Made in the hypothalamus; released from the posterior pituitary
Made in the posterior pituitary; released from the hypothalamus
questions.explanation: ADH is made by neurosecretory cells in the hypothalamus, travels down their axons and is stored in the posterior pituitary, which releases it into the blood. The kidney is its target, not its source.

questions.stem: How does antidiuretic hormone (ADH) reduce water loss in urine?
options: It makes the bladder wall reabsorb water from the stored urine
It makes collecting ducts more permeable to water, so more is reabsorbed
It makes collecting ducts less permeable to water, so more is excreted
It lowers glomerular blood pressure, so no filtrate is formed at all
questions.explanation: ADH causes aquaporins to be inserted into the membranes of collecting duct cells, so more water moves back into the blood by osmosis. The result is a small volume of concentrated urine. Less ADH means fewer aquaporins and more dilute urine.

questions.stem: A hiker drinks no water for six hours on a hot day. Which sequence describes their response?
options: Blood solute concentration rises, the kidneys detect it, less ADH is released, and urine becomes concentrated
Blood solute concentration rises, osmoreceptors detect it, less ADH is released, and urine becomes dilute
Blood solute concentration rises, osmoreceptors detect it, more ADH is released, and urine becomes concentrated
Blood solute concentration falls, osmoreceptors detect it, less ADH is released, and urine becomes dilute
questions.explanation: Losing water by sweating and breathing without replacing it raises the solute concentration of the blood. Hypothalamic osmoreceptors detect this and more ADH is released from the posterior pituitary, so collecting ducts reabsorb more water. Less ADH would produce dilute urine and worsen dehydration.

questions.stem: Alcohol inhibits the release of ADH. What would you expect after a person drinks several alcoholic drinks?
options: A small volume of concentrated urine and a risk of fluid overload
A large volume of concentrated urine with extra glucose in it
A small volume of dilute urine because filtration has stopped
A large volume of dilute urine and a risk of dehydration
questions.explanation: With less ADH, collecting ducts become less permeable to water, so less is reabsorbed and more leaves as dilute urine. The body loses water even though blood solute concentration may be rising. Concentrated urine is the result of more ADH, not less.

questions.stem: What is the cause of type 1 diabetes?
options: Body cells stop responding to insulin, though plenty of insulin is made
The alpha cells make too much glucagon, so blood glucose stays high
The thyroid makes too much thyroxine, so glucose is used too fast
The immune system destroys the beta cells, so little or no insulin is made
questions.explanation: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease in which the body's immune cells destroy the insulin-producing beta cells. Without insulin, glucose stays in the blood. Cells that stop responding to insulin describe type 2 diabetes, which is a different condition.

questions.stem: Why do people with type 1 diabetes need insulin injections rather than tablets that stimulate their pancreas?
options: Their beta cells have been destroyed, so the pancreas cannot be stimulated to make insulin
Their beta cells make plenty of insulin, but it is broken down before it reaches the blood
Their target cells have no insulin receptors, so injected insulin bypasses the receptors
Their alpha cells have been destroyed, so glucagon must be replaced by insulin
questions.explanation: In type 1 diabetes the beta cells are destroyed, so there is nothing left to stimulate; insulin must be supplied. Target cells still have working receptors, which is why injected insulin works. The alpha cells and glucagon are not the cause.

questions.stem: A person with type 1 diabetes injects their usual dose of insulin but then skips a meal and exercises hard. They become shaky, sweaty and confused. What is happening?
options: Hyperglycaemia: blood glucose has risen too high
Hyperthyroidism: thyroxine levels have risen too high
Dehydration: ADH release has been switched off
Hypoglycaemia: blood glucose has fallen too low
questions.explanation: Insulin keeps moving glucose out of the blood while exercise uses glucose and no food replaces it, so blood glucose falls too low. This is hypoglycaemia, treated quickly with fast-acting glucose such as juice or jelly beans. Hyperglycaemia is the opposite, a blood glucose level that is too high.

questions.stem: Which set of symptoms is typical of hyperthyroidism?
options: Weight gain, a slow heart rate and intolerance of cold
Shakiness and confusion that quickly ease after eating sugar
Constant thirst and large volumes of urine containing glucose
Weight loss, a rapid heart rate and intolerance of heat
questions.explanation: Hyperthyroidism means too much thyroxine, which raises metabolic rate: the body burns energy fast, the heart races and the person feels hot. Weight gain, slow heart rate and feeling cold point to too little thyroxine. Thirst with glucose in the urine suggests diabetes.

questions.stem: In Graves' disease, antibodies bind to and activate the TSH receptors on the thyroid. Which test results would be expected?
options: Low thyroxine and high TSH
Low thyroxine and low TSH
High thyroxine and low TSH
High thyroxine and high TSH
questions.explanation: The antibodies stimulate the thyroid directly, so thyroxine is high. High thyroxine then inhibits the hypothalamus and pituitary by negative feedback, so TSH secretion falls. The result is the unusual pattern of high thyroxine with low TSH.
